newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel shekel feud said political.
newsitem.headline: Israel shekel feud said political.

text.p: Israeli analysts and leaders in the economic sector said the issue of widening the shekel's trading bands had turned into a political battle between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Finance Minister Dan Meridor.
Political analyst Hanan Crystal said it was possible Netanyahu was using the economic talks to move on a government shake-up.
"It's all politics...The timing is really classic -- a day after the Bar-On affair ended," Crystal told Israel Radio.
Israel's High Court on Sunday rejected a petition demanding that Netanyahu be indicted for fraud in a decision he said closed the door on a six-month government corruption scandal.
The judges also rejected petitions demanding that Justice Minister Tsahi Hanegbi be indicted or sacked.

Crystal recalled the reports in the last two days that now that the Bar-On affair was over Netanyahu wanted to bring back his former justice minister Yaacov Neeman, who resigned in August ahead of a trial at which he was subsequently acquitted.
That would mean Hanegbi, currently at justice, would move to infrastructure and Ariel Sharon would move to finance from infrastructure, Crystal said.
The analyst said such a plan would leave young Likud leaders like Meridor who might challenge Netanyahu for party leadership outside the government circle.
"He has in essence begun the great battle for the whole kitty," Crystal said of Netanyahu.

Secretary of the Histadrut labour federation Amir Peretz told army radio: "Everyone understands, to my sorrow, that it's all politics. There was no economic move here, only power struggles...If the prime minister wants to do battle with the finance minister, let him do it in his own party and not on the economy's back."
Peretz echoed Meridor's concern that a widening of the shekel's bands would hurt the economy.

"A change in the trading band policy without a correction in the high interest rates set by the governor of the Bank of Israel will put more pressure on all the production sectors in Israel and will create additional pockets of umployment," he said.
Dan Propper, head of the Manufacturers Association, agreed.
"If the trading band is expanded, we'll see higher unemployment and I'm not sure from a social perspective we'll be able to deal with this phenomenon," he told Israel Television.
